A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same misevolution study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Sections 3–4 and the appendices report original safety evaluations, agent trajectories, and memory/tool mitigation experiments across four evolutionary pathways.

after.justification: V2 retains original evaluations and adds longitudinal measurements, ablations, confabulation tests, judge validation, and mitigation experiments. Tables 16–17 explicitly reproduce earlier papers' results, but numerous other results are original.

M1.justification: The underlying evolution frameworks remain unchanged. V2 specifies DPO-based post-evolution alignment and adds a safety instruction inside AFlow's ensemble node, whereas v1 discussed generic safety post-training and inserting guardrail nodes. These are limited adaptations to the mitigation procedures.

E1.justification: V2 adds a nonfunctional-tool scenario using 30 GAIA-inspired cases and approximately 1,300 Memento memories from DeepResearcher (Appendix D.10), plus PKU-RLHF-10K preference data for mitigation training (E.1). The original benchmark and domain coverage largely remains. The additional code/math and OSWorld scores in Tables 16–17 are attributed to prior papers.

E2.justification: The model sets in the original main comparisons are retained. Appendix D.8 newly compares supervised fine-tuning with RL-based self-play, and D.9 directly compares AgentNet memory evolution with AFlow workflow evolution using Qwen2.5-72B on HumanEval.

E3.justification: SALAD-Bench evaluation changes from 1,000 sampled instances to all 21.3k instances. External-tool evaluation changes from 814 to 371 samples, adds filtering for concrete security consequences, and changes the judge from Llama3.1-70B-Instruct to Gemini-2.5-Flash. New longitudinal protocols evaluate 200 training steps and 100 interaction rounds at ten-step or ten-round intervals.

E4.justification: V2 adds longitudinal safety analyses, data-quality and SFT/RL ablations, domain-level case analysis, cross-pathway susceptibility comparisons, nonfunctional-tool confabulation tests, and human validation of tool judgments (Figures 5–6; Appendix D.6–D.11). It also tests model/workflow mitigations and the utility cost of memory mitigation. V1's existing dynamic-memory simulation and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average static AgentNet results over three runs with error bars. V2 clarifies that the retained human-comparison table covers one run, adds Cohen's kappa for tool judgments—0.72 for GPT-4o and 0.82 for Qwen3-235B—and introduces LOWESS trend fitting. No increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Table 6 revises SALAD-Bench and RedCode results; the 7B Coder's initial/evolved RedCode refusal rates change from 100.0%/27.5% to 31.3%/0.6%. AFlow's reported refusal rates change from 46.3%/6.3% to 36.3%/5.6%. Table 3's highest refusal rate changes from GPT-4o-mini's 15.9% to Qwen3-235B's 7.28%, under changed samples and judging conditions. Numerous temporal, utility, ablation, confabulation, and mitigation results are newly reported.

T1.justification: Section 2 retains the same agent-component formalization, evolution function, iterative update, and cumulative-utility objective. The new mechanism discussions and experiments introduce no formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The central novelty claim and four-pathway contributions remain unchanged. However, the introduction revises its quantified risk claims: the memory-related refusal-rate reduction changes from 55% to 45%, and failure to reject malicious external tools changes from approximately 84% to 93%. These refine the claimed empirical magnitude without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes cumulative model-safety decay from incident-triggered memory collapse, develops optimization-pressure and domain-sensitivity explanations, and discusses interactions between memory and tool-failure risks. Appendix B adds substantive deployment guidance. Additional qualifications address DPO's supervision/computational costs and the limitations of post-hoc workflow patches; the earlier general limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies temperatures for AgentNet/tool experiments, DPO's 1,000 preference pairs, and the ensemble mitigation prompt. Many details emphasized in the revised main text, including three SE-Agent rounds and 20 AFlow iterations, already appeared in v1's appendices. The abstract changes its availability statement from 'code and data' to 'code' while retaining the same repository link.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands positioning relative to safe open-ended systems, episodic-memory risks, and multi-agent risks, explicitly presenting this study as an empirical complement to conceptual work. Appendix B additionally connects deployment recommendations to monitoring, tool-security, and memory-defense research. These additions extend the research context beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites setup and mitigation passages, expands explanatory transitions, renames Sections 2 and 4, and moves the standalone Discussion to Appendix A. The appendices are reorganized around deployment guidance, experimental settings, combined results/showcases, and mitigations. This materially changes narrative organization beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 adds temporal plots in Figures 5 and 6(b), a medical-case graphic in Figure 6(a), and a visual summary of the existing deidentification case in Figure 8. It adds the deployment checklist and performance Tables 16–19, relocates the original judge-comparison table to Table 20, updates Figure 3's plotted scales, and adopts conference formatting with widespread figure, table, and code-box reflow.

improvement.justification: V1 relied largely on endpoint safety comparisons and left model/workflow mitigation conceptual. V2 substantially strengthens the study with temporal evidence, mechanism ablations, tool-judge validation, implemented mitigations, and a check that memory mitigation preserves task performance. These address important gaps in empirical support and practical interpretation. Large unexplained RedCode/AFlow revisions and preliminary causal controls limit confidence in some findings, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.
